utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I apologise for the late start of this morning; not the Chamber, but me, myself. If the witness is escorted into the courtroom, Mr. Misetic, you have an opportunity to further re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mrksic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Misetic will now continue his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You recall yesterday we left off discussing General Kovacevic being in Knin on the evening of the 4th of August, and you said that the document that I had shown you refreshed your recollection, that he, in fact, was in Knin on the evening of the 4th. Now, could you tell us, first of all, who Mr. Radic was in the 7th Krajina Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radic was Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know where Mr. Radic was on the morning of the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't able to know the whereabouts of the people in the corps. It was only where a commander would call me, then he would tell me where he was. As for members of his command, I wouldn't know where they were at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe you testified earlier on direct examination that you wouldn't put the entire command in one location; is that correct? When you were talking about breaking up the command into separate rear command, forward command, main command, that there was a reason why you wouldn't put the entire command in one location, can you tell us again why that is?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a general principle in order to make sure that the whole of the command would not perish in a single strike. One could have thought to have elements of the command parish, but if you had nuclear weapons in use or precision artillery weapons, it was not acceptable. Therefore, one had to have a forward command post as well. You asked me about where he, himself, was. I don't know that, not at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, at the transcript page 19054, lines 11 to 12, under Mr. Russo's questioning, you were asked about communications, and you said: "I can see that our communications were easily recorded and transcripts were made." Do you recall saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that yesterday, when I saw that you had -- that it was a plan of the Supreme Command of the Croatian Army and the Intelligence Service, that it was a plan. Until I saw it yesterday, I didn't know that it was a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me show you one of those easily-recorded communications, a transcript. Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit D1257, please. Mr. President, with your leave, I'd like to read it to the witness in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now Croatian Intelligence intercepts of telephone conversation on the 4th of August, and I'd like to turn your attention, on page 2, to a conversation that took place at 7.00 a.m. on the morning of the 4th of August, 1995, right in the middle of that page, right where it says: "We quote the order by General Kovacevic (he is in Knin) to Lieutenant-Colonel Radic, (commander of the BG Dinara)." Let me read it to you in the original: [Interpretation] "Radic, you can only come back dead. You must not come if you leave your position. Here is trouble. They have hit the barracks, too, probably the Slavko Rodic Barracks in Knin. They are pounding everything, and you fuck yourself. Hold on to it however you can. You do not have another country but the Greater Serbia, and you fuck their mother any way you know. I'm telling you in Serbian. Go fuck yourself, hold on, my son, my falcon, and this corps will progress once we have stabilised our state. Did you understand? You can only come back dead, you cannot come alive."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [In English] First, does that refresh your recollection as to where Mr. Radic was on the morning of the 4th and what he was commanding?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection as to where Mr. Radic was on the morning of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the general engaged Radic in that tactical group which was defending the stretch from Grahovo toward Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if Radic was, in fact --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Radic was the last to retreat, according to what I heard at a later date. At that time, I wasn't following the activities by Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but my question to you is: If Radic is, in fact, on Dinara, and you've just said that there's a fundamental principle that you don't have the entire command in one location because it can be taken out by a precise artillery hit --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- do you know where this report says General Kovacevic is at 7.00 a.m. on the morning of the 4th? Does that refresh your recollection as to where Mr. Kovacevic may have been on the morning of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, this document is, as Mr. Misetic has stated, a report, an intelligence report by the HV. The indications in parentheses about where individuals are, are clearly written by the individual who wrote the report. The witness should first be asked if he agrees with the report before it's put to him as a fact of where -- of what's indicated in the report is actually true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, there's some merit in Mr. Russo's observation that the conversation, in itself, doesn't say that much. Therefore, I think we should clearly distinguish between what is said and what is added as comment or explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, two points, then, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First of all, how does Mr. Kovacevic at 7.00 a.m. know that the Northern Barracks, the Barracks Slavko Rodic, has been hit? How does this person know that the Northern Barracks has been hit?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you are confusing the individual with the command. The commander can move about and know everything. However, the command is made up of organs located in a given area. The commander is constantly on the move. From what I see now, the chief was on the Dinara. I forgot this. It was a long time ago. But I'm telling you that Radic retreated from the Dinara during the night and was among the last ones to do so. Now, as for the rest, what was intercepted, who told what to whom and who used what sort of vocabulary, this was not compiled by an officer of mine or anybody else. You know how things are in war. I can't comment on anything here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are political views here of a Greater Serbia, which isn't something that one could hear uttered amongst us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Any knowledge on your part about Mr. Radic wanting to go back into Knin on the morning of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about it. On the 4th, at 22 p.m. [as interpreted], I relocated the command post, and I came to the corps command post, where I left the president was asleep, and I proceeded to Srb. I reached Srb in the morning because it was difficult to move for the crowds of people on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: This is a Croatian intelligence report. Now, you testified yesterday about you don't know why certain things were hit or why certain decisions were made. If you were in General Gotovina's position and received this intelligence report that General Kovacevic is in Knin at the Northern Barracks, would you have fired on the Northern Barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Northern Barracks was hit in the first strike, in the first barrage, as was the command. It was targeted very precisely, and I commented upon it yesterday. Of course, I would target -- I would target all the military targets, as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And even after that first wave, if you found -- if you received intelligence information from your intelligence services that at 7.00 a.m., General Kovacevic is in Knin, communicating with Mr. Radic on the Dinara, would you have continued to fire on the Northern Barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This piece of intelligence refers to an individual and not to the command. I don't think that one would be chasing an individual with rockets either about the town or on the mountains. One uses a sniper for that purpose. That's something else. You see, the Americans have unmanned aircraft that can hit individuals whilst in vehicles, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Since you're still not convinced, let me turn your attention, then, to Exhibit D928, please. If we could turn to page 31 in the English, please. You know who General Sekulic is; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to read this book?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let me state this now. I didn't read a single book or watch a single movie about war, because I didn't want other people's memory to interfere with mine, especially because there were many of those who posed as wise men after the war, in hindsight, a general who is wiser after a battle waged, both in Serbia and in Croatia, and I heard about him writing something. I didn't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page. I'm sorry, page 32 in the English, page 37 in B/C/S, please, starting with the paragraph that says: "A little after 2000 hours ..." If we could turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this portion of Mr. Sekulic's book reports: "A little after 2000 hours, security officer, Captain Dusan Degenek informed Lieutenant-Colonel Radic that the 7th Corps Command chief of security had informed him that their Dalmatian Corps command post had been moved to Padjene village. This shocked Radic. He even wondered how and why the command post was being moved, and he, as Chief of Staff, was not even informed of it. Even then, at about 2100 hours, Lieutenant-Colonel Radic did not know that the whole corps zone had been attacked and that the command post had to be moved because it was impossible to command from Knin." Now, does this portion refresh your memory of when it was that the command of the 7th Knin Corps was moved out of Kinin and into Padjene.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me object, Mr. President. First of all, this is being done under the guise of refreshing recollection. The witness testified that he did not have a recollection about location of the commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: He testified that he did not have a recollection as to individuals in the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, when there is a dispute about what the witness exactly said, the proper way of resolving it is to point at the relevant portion of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try to now find the portion of the transcript. However, as the Prosecution is fond of saying, this is about assisting the Chamber in getting at the truth, and to that extent this portion can be put to him. The witness has said he was led by Mr. Russo to conclusions about how Mr. Kovacevic wasn't in Knin, and when he was shown a document to that effect, the witness said, Now that I have a document in front of me, it does refresh my recollection. There's no point served -- there's no purpose served in trying to cloud the truth, and to that extent --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, my primary objection is to the manner in which it's being done. This is redirect examination, not cross-examination. He's putting matters to him without asking him what his knowledge is. And if his knowledge is different from this, he can't simply put it to him to prove differently, and he can't do it under the guise of refreshing his recollection when the witness doesn't indicate that his recollection needs to be refreshed on the location of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I disagree with that, Mr. President. He specifically, at the end of the day yesterday, said, I didn't have documents in front of me. Now that I have documents in front of me, it does help me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a general statement about the need of refreshment. If that would apply for every single instance is another matter. But if you could find in the record the portion of his evidence he referred to, and then you may put this, which is, by the way, not a document, it's a person writing a book, which of course is a document; I do not disagree with that. But it's a personal account of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just clarify that point. I believe Mr. Sekulic will testify that, in fact, his book is simply a compilation of --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me object to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether or not he will testify, we have not heard his testimony. But you are now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The book is a compilation of reports that were submitted to the Main Staff of the ARSK --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Testifying in front of the witness is not appropriate, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm giving you a proffer as to what the evidence is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Which should not be done in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As Mr. Russo did about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's stop the discussion in this way. I invited you -- I gave you guidance, Mr. Misetic, how you can proceed, and you're invited to do so. If that takes some time, that's fully understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, that's fine. Mr. President, this is -- I have the draft transcript. Mr. President, it's page 19030, beginning at line 12, and your question was: "Did Mr. Kovacevic leave his position at the Dinara slopes, and if so, when?" The witness's answer was: "I would really need to read his report, the one that he submitted, as to exactly when he left, but he probably left during the night, because the following day, during the course of the day ...," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This exactly my objection, Mr. President. The witness pointed out earlier to Mr. Misetic that Mr. Misetic is confusing an individual with the command. Now Mr. Misetic is putting to him ... [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that his recollection needs to be refreshed about the location of the commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're competing and blaming each other for giving testimony. Mr. Misetic, if you would like to refer to certain portions of the evidence of the witness and then put a question to him, and even point at what was written in the book, you can do so. But then take it step by step, clearly setting out what the witness said, whether the portion of the book by Mr. Sekulic in any way refreshes or adds to what is apparently -- or was his memory yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General, have you listened to the portion of the transcript that I read out yesterday, when you said you needed to see General Kovacevic's report as to when he left his position at the Dinara slopes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You should read it again, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, the Presiding Judge yesterday asked you a question. He said: "Did Mr. Kovacevic leave his position at the Dinara slopes, and if so, when?" And your answer was: "I would really need to read his report, the one that he submitted, as to exactly when he left, but he probably left during the night, because the following day, during the course of the day ...," and then it goes on. Now, before we get to that question, I've now -- and you've now acknowledged that, in fact, Mr. Radic was on the Dinara slopes. Would it have made sense for Mr. Kovacevic and Mr. Radic, as to your earlier principle about not putting all the command in one location, for those two gentlemen to be located physically on the Dinara slopes so that they could be taken out by a precise artillery shell? Would that have made sense?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, in that it would not have made sense. If a chief of staff goes to one location, then he should not be followed there by the commander. Likewise, they should not be in the same vehicle, unless such a location is secured. Now, if Kovacevic was there, he was of the mindset that he wanted to show the people that he was courageous, that he was a busy-body. You reminded me that he had come to see me together with brigade commanders for a meeting. Now, where the command was is something that I testified to, because the command included some 30 or 40 officers more. The corps command even had 50 officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, yesterday you testified that you weren't sure whether a portion of the rear command, as you called it, remained in the Northern Barracks. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whether they reached the village of Golubic or stayed behind in the barracks is something I don't know. Nobody sent me these accounts. When a war was being waged throughout Krajina, this was one insignificant matter to know the location of a command. You are putting me in dire straits, asking me about matters that I don't know, and these are matters that, let's say, the commander of the southern area wouldn't know what a company of one of his battalions was doing, or one of his brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, let me then turn your attention -- since you say I'm putting you in dire straits asking you about matters that you don't know, let me see if Mr. Sekulic's book --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- can refresh your recollection on this point, and concerning the portion I read out to you about Mr. Radic being shocked that the command post was being moved and that he, as Chief of Staff, wasn't informed of it, and that the Dalmatian Corps command post had been moved to Padjene village because "the command post had been moved because it was impossible to command from Knin." Now, do you have any recollection of discussions on the 4th about the need to move a command - let's not call it the command - whether it's the rear command, the forward command, the main command, however you want to classify it, whatever it may have been in the Northern Barracks? Do you recall a conversation or discussion of the need to move that command out of the Northern Barracks to Padjene because it had become impossible to command from within Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, throughout the 4th, until 10.00 in the evening, my command was in Knin, and, therefore, it was not logical for that commander to be in Knin. However, just as part of my command went to Srb, part of their command went to Padjene. Now I see that it's called Padjene, that railway station I was referring to. I am not very familiar with the area. I don't know what's in dispute here. The barracks are -- is a military installation. You had assets there that you could not take along. There were vehicles there, and it wasn't abandoned. There were warrant officers and soldiers who stayed behind to take care of the assets there. This is something that every commander would do, and of course the commander went to Dinara, to Padjene, and to a meeting with me with commanders, which doesn't mean that he, himself, is not -- does not represent the command or the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We're in agreement on that point, General, just so you're clear. Okay, we agree. But before you -- hold on, hold on. Let me just ask you this: You said --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you tell me what I am supposed to tell you, and then we are done with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question, then: You said: "Part of my command went to Srb. Part of their command went to ..." Where?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were supposed to go to Padjene, just as mine went to Srb. That's logical. Whether they did or didn't, I don't know, because I didn't keep their time. They would have had to go, because they couldn't stay in Knin and wait for the strike. Just as I expected that I would be the target, I didn't stay at the command post that night, didn't sleep there, they would expect the same thing, that they would be hit or targeted by the forces, or the air force, or the NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where was the 7th Knin Corps Logistics Base in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. I don't even know exactly where mine was of the Main Staff. I just know that they were in Knin, in Golubici, in Strmica, then down the valley of that little river along the railway which Milka Planinc had started moving. That's where we pulled out the reserves, and the vehicles and our assets were dug in there. I can't tell you the details now, but I did observe the deployment and the pullout before the aggression actually started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's try to do this, before I go on: I'd like to ask you to take a look at a map of Knin. Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit P62 on the screen, please. And I'm going to ask you to mark certain locations on the map, based on your best recollection. Using a blue pen, you can actually write on the screen, which you probably are familiar with from your own case.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not blue. Red, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Blue.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then I don't want to write. You are blue, and I was on the red. If you won't accept that, I cannot actually mark this with -- in blue ink to represent myself. I was defending myself, and I was pushed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, we have selected colours in this courtroom so as to know always what marking was made at the request of the Defence and what markings were made at the request of the Prosecution. That's the reason why you were invited to do it in blue. Don't pay too much attention to the colour. Just think as if it was red or green or yellow, but it helps us later on to know whether the marking, sometimes on the same map, was made at the request of the Defence or at the request of the Prosecution. So you would greatly assist us in overcoming your hesitations to use a blue pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, General, are you able to orient yourself on the map at this resolution?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't figure out anything from this map. I don't know if this is Knin or the suburbs. Perhaps you should have written this -- or maybe you can just enlarge it a bit so that I can read, and then I can orientate myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could blow up the bottom half of this map from left to right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this portion of Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the fortress here, the Parliament Building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you locate your own command headquarters on this map?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can see here something that looks like a cross. I don't know what that is, this building at the foot of the Knin Fortress, across from the Parliament and from the railway station. I can't quite determine what this is, because I had never -- I've never seen an aerial photo of Knin. This is the first time that I see it, so perhaps I can be assisted. I don't know whether this is a hotel where the officers stayed, were accommodated. Now, what is the purpose of this exercise? Do you want me to show how well I know Knin or do you want to show me where these features are? You should point them out for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, don't bother too much about what the purpose of the exercise is. Try to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I can't find my way here. I can't figure out what's what. I only see the Knin Fortress here. Should I encircle that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, first try to orient yourself on this map. You said that you saw the fortress a little bit --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's where I had meetings with various representatives of international organisations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you see, a little bit above that, where it's indicated "Parliament," and further up are --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see "Knin Castle."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now further up to the north, do you see something which looks a bit like a railway station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I can, the railway station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you see, a little bit to the right of that, what seems to be a sports field where it's written H-e-l-o, "Helo."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was the helipad, but I never actually used it. This was probably UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but apparently you are aware --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I actually landed at the barracks, and I don't know that it was referred to as a helipad. Maybe this was used by the UN, because they used to land their helicopters there and their delegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not yet at the point where you answer questions. I'm just trying to assist you in orienting yourself. If you would look at the railway station, further to the left, do you see that the road crosses the railway line? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And "General Supply." Okay. Do you see further to the left, a tiny bit further up, that it says "Knin Army Barracks"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the barracks, yes. They called it the Northern Barracks, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's where the corps command was in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you able now to find your way and to understand what this aerial photograph depicts? And I have to tell you that it's always a bit confusing that where usually north is up, here north is to the left. So to that extent --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the left, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see this. This is showing the eastern area, the slopes of the Knin Fortress, where the Presidency was or, as they call it, the Parliament, but for the main part, portions of the army actually met there. And then I can also see the Southern Barracks, where the UNPROFOR forces were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The railway station, which was close to the command, I had actually never been at that railway station, but I knew of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to explain everything you now see on the map, but apparently you were able to orient yourself. Listen carefully to the questions that will be put to you by Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, can you first draw a circle around the Northern Barracks and put an A next to it?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Well, there is a sort of encirclement, because there is the fence all around it, running around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you locate the TVIK factory on this map? Let me try it this way: Can you circle --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must help me a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you circle the railway station and put a B next to it?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you circle the general area of where your command was located? You don't have to be perfect on the building, but just the general area where your command was.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. I think this is it. As far as I can recall, I think this was in the center of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you put a C next to that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, from the railway station, which is B, do you recall which direction the TVIK factory was?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was across on the other side. I think it's the area where the facilities beyond the pole station, as it says. These facilities would have had to -- would have to be the TVIK factory, because it was practically in the town itself. Should I circle that? [Marks]. I never set foot in it, and I never actually visited it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you put a D within that circle, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know where the logistics barracks was or something called the Senjak Barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was also here. As you can see, it's sort of circled. It's to the left of the TVIK factory. It says "General Supply Support." Which letter should I put there, E? [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the MUP police station was?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, well, that, too, was in the town somewhere, but I'm not sure. The ministry, and the organs around it, were together with the command in the area marked C. As for the traffic police and other police, I don't know exactly where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Special Units Corps was quartered in Knin, or a portion of the Special Units Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They came after Grahovo fell; in other words, before the 4th, they had already returned, Stupor [phoen] had returned because his command -- he returned with his corps with a group that he brought in for interventions. They were sent back to Slunj. They never entered Knin. I don't think that he ever came to the command post where I was, because there were urgent matters that I had to deal with; the cutting off of the corps, the joining of the corps with the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where was the PTT?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I was only brought to Knin, by car, to the command post, and I was taken to a house in the town, where I would have my meals, and then I would return in the evening to spend the night there, so I don't know where these institutions were in Knin. I never even went to the hospital, nor did I ever see the UNPROFOR barracks, except for what I could see from the helicopter as I landed at the Northern Barracks. I never used this helipad. So I don't know where the PTT hub was or where the police station was, but I know that most of the forces -- most of the MUP forces and the ministry were in one-and-the-same building. They were on different floors. They had their own security. We did not really mingle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know if the police station had an antenna on the roof?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there were antennas, TV antennas, on every building, I don't even know where the TV was. Although they were under the direct control of the Main Staff, this was something that Kosta Novakovic dealt with. I don't know, I didn't know about it. I spent -- I was there for very brief periods and I had a lot of work to do, so I had to rely on my subordinates. Everyone did their own part of the job. The main thing for me was to avoid the aggression, to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the Stara Bolnica, the old hospital, was?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not the right person to ask those details of. If you were to ask me now where I could -- to find the house where I was accommodated for those 10 days or so, I couldn't actually show you where it was. I just know that I had to walk through the town. It was somewhere -- going from the barracks, I would -- when the shelling started, I would then move to the basement of some buildings and wait for the shelling to stop. It was a private home. I don't know exactly whose it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the MUP or SUP Special Police Platoon was located in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the Dinara. Martic ordered the minister to send them to Dinara because we didn't have personnel. Everyone was on the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where was their base in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, I wouldn't know. Oh, no, excuse me. There was a police base somewhere towards Golubici, when you leave Knin. And it's a good thing that you reminded me of this, because one of my -- one of my assignments when I took over was this: I insisted that this antagonism that existed between the MUP and the army should be overcome, because we cannot change the attitudes and the perceptions among the civilians if, within our own ranks, we go each our own way. And thank you for reminding me of this, because I managed to actually build this relationship so that later on they would join us in some of the fighting at Grebine, on the Dinara, and they even took part in some other assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I remind you of something else as well, Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, do you know where St. Anthony's Monastery is in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know either where Lazarica is or where the St. Ante Monastery is. I didn't have time to go there. I did go once to the Krka Monastery. I went there with the Zagreb bishop, the Italian Zagreb bishop, I believe he's called -- referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just have one moment. Mr. President, if we could have this exhibit marked, and I tender it into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1525.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, I'd like to take you now to Exhibit P2431. Mr. President, this is map 30 in the map binder. And I'm going to show you a map of Knin municipality, General. That's not the map.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are counties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The right map will appear soon. Loading maps takes a bit more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Here we go. If we could blow that up in the area -- the yellow area, the area around Knin, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General, using that blue pen again, can you tell us where the command of the 7th Knin Corps was moved to?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. The railway station here at Padjene, that's where it was. I went there by night and left by night, and that was the only time that I actually went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you put an A next to that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, that road ultimately leads to the Otric Nac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It leads up towards Otric, yes, and then on to Srb, but it's not shown on the map here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the arms depot in the Golubic area was located, looking at this map?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see this road here. There were some minor smaller roads there. They were in these cliffs. I went there once. There was a huge military depot there. It used -- actually, it used to be a depot for the JNA. And I can't recall in detail, but this road going towards Golubici, you would actually enter the depot in a vehicle [marks]. I mean, this is just approximately telling you what it was like, as far as I can recall. But beyond Strmica, where this road was being built, they were pulling out reserves, and we removed from this depot here everything there, because we wanted to make sure that in -- because of the shelling, should they be hit, there would have been a huge explosion and the entire Knin would be just blown up. And this is what we referred to as dispersion of assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, can you identify for us and circle on the map locations where the ARSK had either artillery emplacements or anti-aircraft batteries?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot help you with such details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, I can't recall. I don't know where they shelled from, what positions. I know that we pulled one weapon there, and we tried to provide support to Republika Srpska, which did not react, because up there we had some forces there, a company-strong group, and they used this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter requests that the witness repeat what he is saying, and a bit slower, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the last portion of your answer. You said you tried to provide support to Republika Srpska, which did not react, because up there you had some forces. And could you then finish your answer again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, I don't know. Our forces were there, and they kept asking, from Republika Srpska, that we provide support to them, that we provide a company to them or support them with Orkans. But whatever we managed to recover during the day, overnight it would fall. And then I asked them, Why don't you let me go there with my special corps, and let's see, if I took over command, whether they would be able to advance like that. But then they told me, Well, you can't take command over on our territory. And, of course, what happened then, I've already told you about this. A weapon, 152 millimetres, called Nora, was brought there to Knin Polje, and it was there, I don't know, in Medakovic or Cuge, that area. It was on the foothills of the Dinara, and then towards the shooting range, and from there we shelled Grahovo Polje. Now, what can you do with one weapon? Nothing. We did that while we still had ammunition. But then later on, because this ammunition was scarce, this 152-millimetre ammunition -- it was Russian made. But all of this was at the beginning of the aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Wait for the next question. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1526.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, if we could go, please, back to Exhibit D923. Actually, while we still have this on the screen -- it's more difficult to see. Let's first go to Exhibit D384, Mr. Registrar? Mr. President, I assume we're going until 11.00; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, or close to 11.00 so as to evenly divide the time. How much time would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure at this point. It depends on the answers. I may need another hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you feel that you're not going to make it until 11.00, then please tell me already at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not going to make it. Then I suggest that we have our next break at quarter to, up to 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If we could go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, looking at this map, do you see that on the red circle is Padjene, General?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we go to the right, you see there's something there marked "Barracks Stara Straza"? Were you familiar with what was there at Stara Straza?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not familiar with it. I only knew the name, Stara Straza, but nobody told me specifically what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could now go to Exhibit D923, English page 25, towards the bottom, beginning at numbered paragraph 5. Page 16 in the B/C/S, please at the very bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, again, General Mrksic, this is your report, and it says: "On 5 August 1995, in the morning, the organs of the Main Staff Logistics had found themselves in Srb, where they established a rear command post and made an overview of the logistics support system functioning. Then it was ordered to evacuate 14 railway wagons loaded with ammunition from the tunnel on the axis Stara Straza-Padjene and to relocate them to Otric-Malovan region, in order to take them to the Republika Srpska territory. However, the train personnel and the security left the wagons during the night, but even had they been at their work posts in the morning, it would not have been possible to do anything constructive, since Malovan had already been under the enemy fire." If we go to the next paragraph, please, in the B/C/S on the next page. Now, you report: "In order to initiate destruction of ammunition in the tunnels near Stara Straza, the armoured train was pushed, in order to incite an explosion due to the inertia, and crashed with the wagons loaded with ammunition. This operation failed because the train turned over before the entry into the tunnel. "It was ordered to blow up the mined ammunition store 'Golubic,' and for that all preparations had been carried out previously. But due to the disruption of communications, it was not possible to forward the order to the store commander." Now, General, yesterday you were asked some questions about the railway functioning, and one of your answers was that the armoured train stopped functioning, I believe you said, in 1992. Now, can you explain what the purpose -- first of all, why -- your report says that there, in fact, were train personnel, but they left the wagons during the night. Why was there train personnel employed?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could first object to this. The testimony given during cross-examination related to use of the railways in Knin, and this is -- if Mr. Misetic wants to point to the transcript, we will see from the transcript references what that discussion was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is not a proper objection, and as far as I know, railways don't operate within 500 metres, they go someplace, and that's the next area where I'm taking him on my cross, and the objection is totally improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The objection, Mr. President, is that this does not arise from cross-examination. This is simply an attempt to correct problems during his direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's absolutely untrue. As a matter of fact, Mr. President, we can look at P804, which is an ECMM report, where I was going to take him next, which says train are seen being moved in Knin. Now, I'm entitled to go into redirect and put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I don't know why he didn't simply start with the ECMM, rather than taking him to areas where I didn't cover and ask him about those areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But since he'll go there, the objection still stands?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That depends on whether we're going there now or if he's going to continue with this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, anyway you could proceed in such a way that you could do it uninterrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I'm entitled to show the railways had 14 wagons full of ammunition. Mr. Russo may not like it. That's certainly his issue that he can raise. But what are the trains doing in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may continue your line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If I could just -- Mr. President, the question, What are they doing in Knin, the question has not been put to the witness where these were. The document he's been shown does not indicate they were in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I said, there's an ECMM report. It will be shown to the witness. But first we're entitled to explore the use of the railway system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General, I'm just going back to my question. Why was train personnel employed in the Stara Straza-Padjene axis?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was probably down to the Logistics Base to pull out these assets. Since the railway was not damaged, it could have been used, some 20 to 30 per cent of it. I know that trains were not running through Knin; maybe locally. I didn't hear the noise of the trains, and I didn't use one, and nobody -- I never heard anybody say I was going to go to Lapac by train. As for the armoured train, this was some contraption that was produced at the beginning of the war, and nobody got what the point was. What did they want to achieve by it? Some sort of an explosion. That didn't make any sense. This probably served as justification for the fact that ammunition had been left there. You know how people want, for the sake of history, to rectify certain matters by providing explanations. Somebody must have compiled the document and given it to me for signature. I don't know if it bears my signature or not. Well, I don't see what is controversial there. If there were empty carriages, then they could have been used to pull the ammunition out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me make sure I understand your testimony. General, this is -- this is your report, Exhibit D923, and you say that -- page 31, lines 12 and 13 -- sorry, 11 through 13: "This probably --" this -- and you're referring to the portion I read from your report: "This probably served as justification for the fact that ammunition had been left there. You know how people want, for the sake of history, to rectify certain matters by providing explanations."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course. I would have preferred that it had not been left there, but we can't escape the fact that it was, and that's why I'm here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General, if I could turn your attention to Exhibit P804, please. If we scroll down to section 4 of this report, which is the next page in the B/C/S. General, this is a report from the ECMM on the 4th of August, and you can see in point 4 it says : "Obviously, a lot of damage during the day. Trains are seen being moved in Knin. Comment: Presumably used for military purpose, but could these be used for the evacuation of civilians?" Now, do you recall seeing trains moving in Knin on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing trains. If they were moving, then the purpose of it was to pull out ammunition, since trains were workable up to the point where depots were located. As for the civilians, themselves, I don't know how far they could have been evacuated by trains. They were evacuated by buses, by private vehicles, others on foot, still others asked their neighbours to give them a lift, or whatever could be found as means of transport was used. This is the first time I hear of an interpretation of the evacuation of civilians as being done by trains. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could now have 65 ter 1D1082, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a few questions about the TVIK factory that you were asked about yesterday, General. And if we look at the English -- the first page is a cover page, signed by -- or for Assistant Commander Mirko Bjelanovic, where he is forwarding a document of the Main Staff, dated 11 June 1995, in which the Main Staff requested modification of aerial bombs so they could be launched by the Kosava LRST M-94. It says the attack will be carried out by Banijametal, work organisation in Dvor na Uni, with whom a contract on the modification should be written up. If you turn the page, it's the attached letter. It's signed by -- if we turn the page in the B/C/S. It's signed by you.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the signature. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's coming up, General.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This isn't my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell what is written there in type?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Mile Mrksic," but my signature never looked like this one. I don't see what is controversial here, other than the fact that this isn't my signature. Shoot any questions you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just point out that paragraph 2 of this document, if we could go back one page in the English, now it says in paragraph 2: "Upon completing the manufacture of 75 bombs by the Banijametal RO in Dvor na Uni, hand them over in units according to the following schedule." And one of the units is the 7th Knin Corps, the 15th Corps, and then below that it says remaining bombs are to be stored in the Golubic depot. Now if we could go to -- now, this is as of 12 June.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, the signature we see in the right-hand corner -- now you've taken it off the screen. This isn't my handwriting or my signature or initials. Can we go to the top of the page, please? "Chief of the Technical Service."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've had it translated as "Dobrijevic" on the top corner.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the man, and this isn't my signature. It must have been done through someone else. Let's see what the gist is and what you want me to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Hold on. Let's look at two more documents, and then I'll ask you the question. General, let's look at Exhibit D950.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we agree that I didn't sign the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, you testified that it's not your signature. We don't have to reach agreements between witnesses and the parties. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, this is now Exhibit D950. This is 10 July, and now it makes reference to that company that's in the previous document, Banijametal at Dvor na Uni, and it says: "Due to the urgent need of constructing lethal devices to be launched from an earth-bound rocket launcher and given the capacity of the TVIK factory - Knin - we have allocated part of the production of certain products in cooperation with the Banijametal factory. Dvor na Uni, to the aforementioned factory." And then the third paragraph says: "I propose that the TVIK factory - Knin - be put into the work system of the Sector for Military and Special-Purpose Production, at least for a certain period of time and that the requirements of the sector for military and special purpose production be considered a work priority." And now let me turn your attention to another document. Mr. Registrar, this is D444, please. This is an order for air defence, an operational order, dated 13 February 1995. The introductory paragraph -- and this is of the command of the 7th Knin Corps. It talks about anticipated attacks, and it says: "In the corps defence area, approximately 24 sorties of combat aircrafts may be expected ..." And if we go into paragraph 2, it says: "The focus of the operation is to be expected on the following axes:" And it gives the axes, and then it says: "... with the attack directed on the positions on artillery units for support and anti-armour combat, on the armoured mechanised units, Knin town, and the structures in the town such as the General Staff of the Serb Army of the Krajina, the TVIK factory, the military barracks, et cetera ..."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hydro plant Obrovac, Manojlovac, and the storage sites at Golubic. Yes, that's right that was an assessment of what was to be expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I've shown you those documents about, at least, which purport to show at least some intent for production of military supplies in the TVIK factory. My question to you is: Why would the 7th Knin Corps have anticipated an attack by the HV on the TVIK factory?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, every factory -- well, why did NATO strike all of our factories during the aggression? Whatever could be used for certain purposes was declared a military target. If you look at nuts and bolts individually, then they don't serve a purpose, but if you put them to use, then they could also be used for military purposes. But the factory did not produce a rifle, a bomb, or any explosive. It was natural for any country to have a factory that would be producing goods that could be used for other purposes, and then, of course, you have assembly factory as well. Well, look at what we had in Slavonski Brod. You had parts produced across Yugoslavia which would then be assembled in Slavonski Brod. And I didn't know of anything being assembled to that effect in TVIK factory, because they would have invited me, as a commander, to make a tour of the factory. It was important for the workers, and even today it is important for the residents of Knin. It was the largest nut-and-bolts factory in former Yugoslavia, with cutting-edge technology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would tender 65 ter 1D1082.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: We'll object, Mr. President, based on the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you assign a number so that the document be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1527, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Misetic, perhaps we could first ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back after the break, Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A break, right. I thought it was all over, and I was surprised that we finished so soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could you give us an estimate on how much time you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Forty-five minutes or less, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I like the "or less" rather than the 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you try to finish in half an hour. Then I take it the Cermak Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Russo, as matters stand now?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: As matters stand now, Mr. President, I don't have anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we'll break now and resume at 20 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Mrksic. Mr. Misetic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, may we please have 1D1048 on the screen, please, page 16 of the B/C/S, page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, this is a report that you can see on your screen, on the right-hand side, purporting to be sent on the 4th of August from you to the Yugoslav Army, General Staff, Air Force and Air Defence Sector. I don't think we have the right translation on the screen. There we go. And if you look at the stamp on the bottom, and if we can scroll down on the original, it says it was received at 1300 hours on the 4th of August. Now, can you explain this document for us? It talks about the following means of communication have been destroyed/disabled, and "we are requesting replenishment." Can you explain what types of communication were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the PVO and RV system, the equipment for their systems. The RRU 800 was, at the time, the key instrument for communications. It was a long-range device. The RRU 1 are radio relay devices, one-channel devices. The gentlemen know that. The radio station or radio unit 100, that's 100 kilometres, its range. The IFP-PKON, this is very technical, it's probably a wire -- or land wire system of communications. And UKP are cables or wires. These -- actually, these devices were destroyed during the first -- in the first barrage of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I ask this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1528. THE COURT: And it is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. President, this is part of that long exhibit and we will upload only the pages. So, for the record, it is -- the portion is Exhibit D1048, that is page 16 in the B/C/S and page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. -- I'm sorry. General, let me show you another map. This is 65 ter 4865. It is map 20 in the binder of maps. Now, this is a map of the Gracac municipality, and you can locate in the middle of the screen the word "Gracac." And if we go -- you'll recall yesterday you had some question as to the location of Bruvno. If you go -- take that road that goes north from Gracac, you'll see --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That is where the -- you had located a portion of the Special Unit Corps, the KSJ, before Storm; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a portion of the brigade, yes. This was the theatre -- landing theatre for interventions to the left and to the right, that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if you were going to deploy them from Bruvno, let's say to get to Knin to assist on the Dinara, or to go to Mali Alan to assist in the breakthrough where the Croatian Special Police were breaking through, would they have to go through that junction, through Gracac, and then go left or go right, to get to --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right, but I think the intersection -- because I took this road a number of times, the intersection or the cross-road is before Gracac, if you're headed towards Knin. The road actually forks earlier on, but if you were to take the pass -- the mountain pass towards -- towards whatever, of course then you would have to go through Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So these were the axes of possible interventions. You've noticed this quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I wasn't sure if this map was in evidence or not. I thought it was, by agreement of the parties. But if not, I'll tender it, and perhaps we can MFI it. And if it is, then obviously we don't have to put it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I don't object to the exhibit. I'm just paying attention to the transcript, the page 39 to 25, to page 40 through 5, I think there were some words missing about how he described the precise location of the intersection which don't appear on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what's missing at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, but I would have one question. You were describing the fork. Coming from Bruvno, going to the south, just before you arrive at Gracac town, where you turn -- you turn to the right and will then arrive --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the left, to the left, towards Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, to the left, towards Knin, avoiding that you have to pass through Gracac town. And if you turn to the right, you have, I think, two options. One is going through town, itself, and another one going --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and one is going around Gracac or along Gracac. That's how the main road actually used to run, if you're going to the seaside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's now clear to me, because where exactly the fork was -- and that, I take it, you want to draw our attention especially to the crossroads, or the fork, as the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, Mr. Russo, you're satisfied that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if not in evidence, I don't know whether we ever admitted the whole -- I don't think the whole series, but --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't show that this specific 65 ter number is in evidence, so this will become Exhibit D1529.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, D1529 is admitted into evidence. I again urge the parties, now it is not dramatic here, if you use maps, use maps which really reflects what's on the ground and not the stretched ones, because all the proportions, and that's true with all these maps, are just wrong. But for the purposes today, it doesn't make much of a difference. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's my confusion, because Mr. Markac and I had actually sat down and selected 30 that we all agreed were going, so I was unaware that, ultimately, they did not all going in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you compare them with proper maps, you'll see that they're all stretched. That means that the distances, horizontally or vertically, are not reflecting the real distances. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, I want to turn your attention to this issue of encirclement. And first if I could ask that 65 ter 2326 be brought on the screen. Now, General Mrksic, were you aware that the Security Council passed a resolution concerning the events in Croatia on the 10th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of August, 1995? At the time, I was already in Banja Luka and dealing with totally different problems, so I had no idea what was going on in the world. I didn't receive any newspapers, nor was I briefed on it, nor was there anyone who could brief me, because at the time we were practically disintegrating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the simple answer was, no, you were not aware?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 of the Security Council -- no, sorry. Yes, page 2. It might be page 3. It is page 3, I'm sorry, under point 2. Your Honour, it appears that the B/C/S document is not the same as the Security Council resolution on the screen, so I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have to have that corrected. Let me just read out the one portion that's of interest to me, General, and that is the Security Council demanding, amongst other things, that the Government of the Republic of Croatia, under point A, respect fully the rights of the local Serb population, including their rights to remain, leave, or return in safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Super. Yes, well, this was before the aggression. Had this happened before the aggression, it would not have gone the way it did, but -- that would have been perfect, but, unfortunately, in practice it didn't happen. This is exactly what we were aiming for. That's why I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question is: You did, ultimately, have some knowledge of what did happen in Sector North, for example, with Mr. Bulat. Were you aware of the general position of the international community, that the Republic of Croatia should respect the rights of the local Serb population to leave, if they wished?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any knowledge of these paragraphs, nor did I have any communications, and I was in no communication with the encircled 1st Corps. My connection or my communication was when I ordered that the tanks be pulled out so that the T-84s do not fall into the enemy's hand. And then I withdrew to Dvor, and I fought there in order to prevent the people, the civilian population, being massacred in Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand the witness's answers, but on the assumption that there's no dispute that this is the resolution of the Security Council, I'd ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's more or less a Bar table submission, because the witness apparently has no knowledge or -- and was even a bit confused when he said this was before the aggression, since the date was the 10th. But, Mr. Registrar, could you assign a number to this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I would like to say something else. I would like to change what I've said. I would have liked this to have been before the aggression, but you understood me to say that this actually was before the aggression. This is -- this was my wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's now fully understood. Reading this, you say if this only would have happened before what you call the aggression. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1530.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1530 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General, let me ask you some questions. You are an officer who was trained at the highest levels in the Yugoslav Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct, and I became a general during the SFRY, the same way that President Tudjman became general, except he had become a general much earlier. But we went to the same schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What was the highest level of military education that you received?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The War College and the Operations School. We used to call it the War School or War College, but it changed -- it had changed its name into the Operations School. That's where I graduated from, because this is the school where we actually studied large operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you, in your military education, have an opportunity to study military history?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as the instructors, and the lecturers provided us with these, but, of course, as any young man, I was interested in reading up on the history of my own nation, but not in any particular special courses, and I wasn't really very much into history.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you some questions based on an answer you gave at transcript page 19080, line 4, which I believe is Mr. Russo citing earlier testimony of yours. And this is related to your point that -- but you didn't just cut us off. And I'm going to -- for example, let me just ask you: Have you heard of some of the great military works -- Sun Tzu --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sun Tzu Wa, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Vegetius, the principle of Scipio? Let me show you on the screen, General. This is via Sanction. Let me -- Sun Tzu is a 6th century Chine general who wrote --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You have to do something so that the enemy actually does what you want him to do. In that sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One of the other great books of military history is from Roman times, and let me show you. And I'm going to ask to read this portion to you from the great works of military history and ask you whether you agree with it, and this is via Sanction. This is now Flavius Vegetius Renatus on Military Matters, Book 3. One of the maxims is: "The flight of an enemy should not be prevented, but facilitated." And he wrote thousands of years ago: "Generals unskilled in war think a victory incomplete unless the enemy are so straightened in their ground or so entirely surrounded by numbers as to have no possibility of escape. But in such situation, where no hopes remain, fear itself will arm an enemy and despair inspires courage. When men find they must inevitably perish, they willingly resolve to die with their comrades and with their arms in their hands. The maxim of Scipio, that a golden bridge should be made for a flying enemy, has been much commended. For when they have free room to escape, they think of nothing but how to save themselves by flight, and the confusion becomes general; great numbers are cut to pieces."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually, this is exactly what I would like to comment on. This is perfect for my purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "The pursuers can be in no danger when the vanquished have thrown away their arms for greater haste. In this case, the greater the number of the flying army, the greater the slaughter. Numbers are of no signification where troops, once thrown into consternation, are equally terrified at the sight of the enemy as at their weapons. But on the contrary, when men shut up, although weak and few in number, become a match for the enemy from this very reflection, that they have no resource but in despair." Now, General, that's a principle, I assume, that you're very familiar with, as a general who passed through military education, you should leave a golden bridge for your enemy to flee; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, don't put the question to me like that. You've read the text for like 20 minutes by this Flavius whoever, a military theoretician from days of Rome, but I wouldn't go that far back into time. Let's go back to World War II. It is true that once you put a cork in the bottle and there is no way out, then the cost is very high. Every soldier knows that. Don't preach to me or don't teach me. I didn't understand you to be doing that, but thank you very much for putting this up or raising this issue, because I would like to say something to the Court. We all know that the enemy should never be brought in despair, because, first of all, that would cause a lot of your own victims and losses, because it does not allow the enemy any other option but to fight to the death. If they do not believe in who they are fighting against in their moral integrity, in their keeping to the international rules of law, you're right, then they would sell their skin highly. And you're absolutely right. When I was on my first wartime assignment at Vukovar, I kept a road open throughout this time towards Vinkovci.
