Had I shut off that way out, Vukovar would have fallen in a day.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter kindly requests that the witness repeat the last portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, General, the interpreter did not hear the last few sentences.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will reiterate it slowly. What you have said here -- all right. Whenever the purpose is not to destroy the enemy, to destroy his manpower, then you must always leave a road for the enemy to pull out. However, if the goal is to conquer a territory, regardless of what happens to the enemy, then that escape route should be so wide that the enemy doesn't give it a second thought but use it. So you should never put the enemy in a situation where he has to fight instinctively and to fight to the death. That's the role of every commander. But I would like to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I just consulted with my colleagues --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because this is a scientific sort of position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether it's scientific or not, whether it's, to some extent, military philosophy, whether, to some extent, it is military history, where military philosophy, perhaps, not always matches with military history, especially if we are then soliciting -- I'm not saying that you sought that, Mr. Misetic, but if elements of other cases get involved, then the Chamber is not assisted by that and would like you to focus again on what is relevant for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I had no intention of getting into any other cases before the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but that's, to some extent, what might have happened. And there again, history and philosophy, how important it may be, has no direct bearing on this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it was only raised with respect to the answer that I cited the transcript for. So if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you, but we let you go for a while, we let the witness go for a while, and now we move on to other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. President, as a matter of fact, I've completed it, my examination. General, I want to thank you for coming and testifying, and I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. The position the same, Mr. Kay; no questions for the Cermak Defence. Mr. Mikulicic, no questions from the Markac Defence. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, I have a few questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first have on the screen D923. Yes. Mr. Mrksic, quite a lot of questions have been put to you in relation to this report. You remember that --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you testified about it. You pointed out to us what your position was in relation to Mr. Perisic, to Mr. Mladic. Could we move to the last page of this document. Mr. Mrksic, I think you also testified that the signature under this document is yours. And, finally, you testified that you had seen this document only here for the first time, I think you said. Now, do you have an explanation, because you said something, this is not the type of document -- who would have drafted it -- one second, please. It should be mention now. How could it be that, on the one side, you recognise your own signature; and at the same time you say, "I see it in court for the first time"? I have trouble reconciling those answers.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm confused, Mr. President. My officers knew of this, and I was -- my officers were not just lower-level officers. They were the chief of the operations - he was a general - and colonels. They all knew that they should not put before me a document of this type for me to sign, where you can't see where -- who the document was typed by, who it was drafted by, whom it was sent to, where it was filed. In my life, I've never seen anything like this. From when I became the Chief of Staff at brigade level up until the top, I never allowed this type of document to be shown to me for signing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time -- that's what you explained before, you wouldn't allow this to happen. It appears that it either happened, or it's a forgery, or whatever, but what is for you the explanation that you say, "I see this document now for the first time; nevertheless, I recognise my signature"? Could it be that you have been inadvertent at the time and that you just signed it without properly looking at it, or what is your explanation for it? It's a long document.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is long, and whoever brought it to me would know that I wouldn't sign this, because I would first look at the left-hand side of the document and then I would read the rest. But how this was done technically and how a signature could actually be reprinted, I don't know. But I do recognise the content, and it's strange to me that a document of this importance, that I would send it to the chief of the Main Staff without such indications on the document. Either I have gone off my mind or somebody else has. But as a matter of course, I did not allow this. I was an officer of the Main Staff, so there would have to be also the principle where a document had to have a brief description so I wouldn't have to read the entire document. This was actually introduced into practice by General -- by Generals Mamula and Kadijevic, that that was the proper procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But to summarise, you say whether someone cheated or "whether I have been inadvertent," you do not know. It's your signature, and, nevertheless, you have no recollection to have seen it at the time, and your recollection is you first saw it in court?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. And, of course, a signature can be copied onto any piece of paper. It can easily be done nowadays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it can. But you do not exclude for the possibility that you signed it and not sufficiently --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then next move to P480. Perhaps it could be taken from the screen a second. Could we take it from the screen one second. Mr. Mrksic, you testified in quite some detail as to orders for evacuating the population of certain areas, how that decision was reached and how that order was sent to those who had to implement it. Could you tell us, was this order, was this distributed among the population in any way directly?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As it says, the order was sent to civilian structures of municipalities and it wasn't sent to the population at large. There was no direct address by the president of the republic to the people. Subsequently, my mother told me that they had been disseminating leaflets to the effect that we had been dissolved, killed, et cetera, et cetera. I saw it just for a moment before you took it off the screen here. That was part of the propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said flyers -- and I'm now referring to your testimony, not necessarily in relation to what was just on the screen. You said, during your testimony, flyers were being thrown around. Could you explain what you referred to at that moment when you gave this testimony? What flyers were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was printed material with instructions ostensibly on my behalf. They were issued by someone from the staff or the republic itself. It was an old system dating back to World War II, when television and mass media were not as developed as they were today. That's what they resorted to as an option, and they were distributed -- thrown around, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said: "... ostensibly on my behalf. They were issued to someone from the staff or the republic itself." Did you mean to say that the system was such that they would be issued by someone or whether that happened in this specific case?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you misunderstood me. It was probably the propaganda machinery of the Main Staff of Croatia or some other propaganda system that they had. They issued such flyers and instructions on our behalf, not that someone would be betraying me. That would be difficult without me noticing it, and of course they would have to have a reason. I had good officers, and nobody proved to be traitors. Perhaps they were -- there were collaborators with the enemy side among them that I wasn't aware of, but they also had some of ours on their side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you are aware of this evacuation order to be broadcasted; radio, television? Are you aware of any such broadcasting of the evacuation order that apparently was reached on the afternoon of the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's when it was taken, and at around 5.00 or 6.00 p.m. it was distributed to the municipalities in Dalmatia. That's as far as it went. It didn't go to the areas of Luka -- Lika, Kordun, and Banija. Now, whether this was broadcast by some faked TV station or not, I couldn't tell you, because I didn't watch TV. I looked out of the window, observing the shelling of Knin, and I was awaiting reports from my subordinates. And in the meeting, I had a meeting with the Lika and Dalmatia Corps to see what was to be done next, once such a decision on the withdrawal was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, you talked about TV, not about radio. Did you -- apparently not yourself, but did you hear anyone telling you that they heard this evacuation order to be distributed by radio broadcast?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that. Kosta Novakovic, the commissar -- or, rather, he was assistant for moral guidance and information. He had direct control over the media outlets. He did not have such an approval for this to be made public, because then third parties, including the enemy, could have heard it and abused the information in such a way that they would launch an all-out attack. We didn't go public with it. It wouldn't have been natural for such an order to be made public. Still, I can't make any assertions, because I didn't listen to the radio and I didn't watch TV. According to my understanding of the commander and the Presidency, this was supposed to be done in a covert manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we go back to P480. First question to you: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time. Thank you for showing it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever give an order as presented in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you earlier talked about flyers, this document, does say it is to be distributed by leaflet, is this the type of document you had in mind or --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under "flyers," I mean pieces of paper containing instructions being thrown out of aircraft. This is what is implied by the term "flyer." A flyer would not be understood to be the sort of material that would be distributed by hand. In that case, you would talk about secret dispatches. A flyer is a public document which is disseminated by air. And when you say fake flyers or flyers for propaganda purposes, then it is clear what is meant by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that you had not seen this document before. Had you heard about this document to exist and being distributed -- for it to be distributed?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that flyers were being thrown. I heard it from civilians who had pulled out across Dvor na Uni into Republika Srpska. Whenever I saw civilians, they would point at me and say, There is the commander, it's not true that he's dead. So this is obviously something that the population was informed of and something that the population believed; in other words, that I had been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Have the questions by the Bench triggered any need for further questions, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If we could go, Mr. Registrar, to Exhibit D106, please. Further Re-examination by Mr. Misetic:

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General, your answers to the Judge's questions about whether this was broadcast to the public, D106, I'm taking you back to your interview with Radio Belgrade on the 4th of August, 2130. And in your first paragraph of your first answer, you say: "The aggression which commenced at 0500 hours lasted until the nightfall. At the present, all combat activities in the area of Knin have ceased. Knin is engulfed by the dark, evacuation of the population is ongoing, enemy forces reached at four to six kilometres from the city of Knin." If we go down a few paragraphs to that long paragraph that says: "HV was successful on the direction ..." Towards the middle, you say: "Presently, we are engaged in the evacuation of the population from Dalmatia, to prevent them from falling captive, because Knin and the communications leading from Knin are in danger." Now, in your answer to Judge Orie, you said that you thought that this was a covert operation to evacuate. Could you explain to the Court why you were on the radio on the evening of the 4th, however, speaking about the fact that you were in the process of evacuating the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was I who spoke here, and I don't remember, I never spoke to journalists. Perhaps the individual didn't introduce himself as a journalist. I don't recall ever saying something that it would subsequently be broadcast by Radio Belgrade. I don't recall giving any interviews. I am reputed to be a person who does not give interviews. That's why I find it strange that I should have given an interview to anyone. Perhaps I spoke to someone on the phone without realising that the person would misuse what I said for their purposes. And had a journalist told me that he was seeking an interview from me, I would not have given it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me now draw your attention to Exhibit D1516, page 2, please. And if we go to page 2, please. Now, this is General Kovacevic's report again. Now, General Kovacevic, at paragraph 6, the second paragraph of number 6, says: "In the course of the 4th of August, the RSK government issued a public statement, calling the entire population in the endangered areas to evacuate, which caused a chaos within the units and their dispersion, because ..." Do you see that, General? It's on the next page. I'm sorry, it's on the next page for you in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says -- sorry, it's on the previous page, on the bottom, I guess. If we could scroll up, please, if we could scroll up. There we go, right at the top: "In the course of the 4th of August, the RSK government issued a public statement calling the entire population in the endangered areas to evacuate, which caused a chaos within the units and their dispersion, because the soldiers started leaving in order to go home and help their families with the evacuation." 25 Mr. Registrar, if we could now go to Exhibit D928, at page 23, please. Now, I believe this is page 36 in the B/C/S. If we could go one back, please, in the B/C/S. I'm sorry, if we could go to page 26. There we go. In the middle of the page in the B/C/S. Now, General Sekulic's book says: "The decision of the Supreme Defence Council was announced to the public at 2000 hours on 4 August. It went to the people and through UNPROFOR to the Croatian Army and Tudjman's state. It reads as follows:" And then it proceeds to quote the announcement. The next paragraph says: "The Supreme Defence Council appeals to the Krajina citizens, where evacuation is being organised, not to undertake individual actions or be fooled by the Croatian propaganda. The citizens may contact Civilian Protection officers for any information." Now, General, these passages, do you know what type of announcement, if any, General Kovacevic is referring to and General Sekulic is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. You'll have to ask them about it. I didn't read the book. Were there any announcements, or through whom? Well, they did state here that they shouldn't be fooled by the propaganda and that they should apply to their Civilian Protection officers in their localities, to avoid panic, because panic was widespread. Are the cars going to start up, do they have enough fuel, et cetera? We knew that where such a decision could be taken, a grave situation may arise. I could not have taken something of the sort upon myself. That's why the Supreme Council had to decide about it. Who could provide us with any guarantees if we are in an encirclement and in a position where we had to fight in an encirclement, whilst cut off from anywhere else? You see that the same rules of engagements that General Tudjman was taught by, that a force needs to be designated in every village to protect the population, and such a commander who is in charge of the town command is superior to any other commander who might wish to transit that particular area, because what one has to ensure is that the population is not harmed. That's something I was aware of in Eastern Slavonia. Had I known that you had all these various weapons systems and had I known that you were trained by the Americans, my idea was that -- and they knew, of course, that the children had to be distributed with chocolate, et cetera, that they had to be adjusted or adapted to the idea of coexistence, that was what I aimed at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, apart from answering the question, you gave your personal views and messages to us as well, which are not directly relevant in answer to the question. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just follow up on your answer, General. You talk about --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'd like to know is: Can that be found somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, if you tell me what it is I should be looking for, I'll look for it, and that's why I'm following up here. You say that -- this is at page 59, lines 4 through 10. You see the same rules of engagement that General Tudjman was taught by, that a force needs to be designated in every village to protect the population, and such a commander who is in charge of the town command is superior to any other commander who might wish to transit that particular area, because what one has to ensure is that the population is not harmed. Now, I'm interested -- can you, first, explain what you're referring to about a commander in every village?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to object to this. The Court's questions clearly related to the dissemination of a piece of information. We're now getting into areas which the Court did not get into.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness gave an answer, and as I said before --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking this only because the Court raised an issue about dissemination of information, and I believe that the witness's answer was given in that context. And to avoid any confusion, the witness should clarify the chain and how certain information may have been distributed, and that's the only purpose of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've had testimony from the witness about what he knows about how this information was disseminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- sometimes putting the question to the witness takes less time than to -- if it is already in evidence, then there's no problem. If it adds anything that could assist the Chamber, you may put the question. But, at the same time, the last answer, where, after two lines you had the answer already, you let the witness go for another 15 lines, so if you could keep it focused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, you heard what my question was, which was your reference to commanders in every village, and in order to cut this short: Were you suggesting that the commanders in the village would have received the information about the evacuation order?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, you misinterpreted my entire intervention. What I was saying was that had been in the shoes of the general here who launched the attack, he was duty-bound, for Strmica and for all the other places, to designate a commander and to make sure that the local population cooperated with the commander and was protective of him, so that it could not be possible for a situation to arise where you would have a policeman entering the village and doing whatever he wanted at will. This is something that we were taught in the combat rules of the JNA, which you inherited and which President Tudjman studied perhaps even more than I did, and it should have been applied, not to speak of the American rules which the gentlemen were taught about at the courses they attended. They went even further than the JNA doctrine. That's what I meant. You misunderstood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood your earlier answer as a bit on the abstract level as well. You are not seeking to enter that area. The witness gave a rather abstract answer, where I was primarily interested in what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's what I was interested in, too, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but by abstract answers, you might not find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions? If not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're nearing the end?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can only say we, and I'm looking to everyone in the courtroom, we made it in time. Mr. Mrksic, usually I thank witnesses for coming a far way to this courtroom. There's no need to do that. Nevertheless, I would like to thank you very much that you came to this courtroom and that you had answered I wouldn't add "at length," but you've answered --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More than necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and that were put to you by the Bench. Thank you very much, and I'll ask you now to be escorted out of the courtroom. Mr. Domazet --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I'd like to thank you also for being available at such short notice, and being able to meet the concerns Mr. Mrksic had at the time. Thank you. Mr. Mrksic, you'd like to add something. Short; no messages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no messages. I would like to thank you for your consideration. You realise the situation I was in. This was my first public appearance. I never gave any testimonies or interviews for TV or radio. And to thank Mr. Misetic, Defence counsel for Gotovina, who was insistent upon ensuring my appearance here. I managed to relieve myself of some burdens; not of all of them. And I would like to thank the Defence for raising certain interesting matters related to security, which will only be discussed; to the Prosecutor, who was quite brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware that the Chamber still has to decide on D1508, which is MFI'd at this moment. Mr. Mikulicic, there was one document that you have tendered, but I think it's not assigned a number yet. It was the document in which some allegations were had as to involvement in smuggling, et cetera. Could you please repeat the ID number of that document so that it can be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a document 65 ter 3D00126. And, Your Honour, with your permission, while I'm on my feet, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the document already tendered into the evidence, and that is D1495, is referring to the documents that I was intending to tender, and it is my belief that for the sake of complicity, both documents should be entered into the evidence, while the one is for the moment and the other one is pending. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said "complicity." I take it for completeness sake, you wanted to refer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will look at that, because there was objection against, if I could call it, the smuggling document, isn't it, Mr. Russo, as irrelevant? And the witness denied any of its content. Let me just have a look. The Chamber will, in due course, decide on these exhibits, but first a number has to be assigned to 3D00126. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1531, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We'll have a break. Is the Gotovina Defence ready to call its next witness? Mr. Misetic, I have some concerns about the days to come, because the next witness has been scheduled for one and a half hours in-chief, although there's a rather lengthy 92 ter statement. Do you have any other witnesses ready before Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we do not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll, nevertheless, ask whether there is already at this moment any estimate of how much time the other Defence teams would need for the examination of the witness which will appear after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It depends what happens in direct examination, but at the moment, I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is the very same position for the Markac Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo -- or should I address Ms. Mahindaratne? Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe I estimate about four hours of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means it would take us most likely into Thursday. Thank you for that information. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, before the Chamber will invite you to call your next witness, I first would like to inform the parties that Monday we'll not be sitting. That was already announced as the most likely outcome, but that's now confirmed. The Chamber received, for the next witness, the 92 ter statement, and if there's anything problematic with the translation, we'd like to be informed about it early, because it's a lot of double work for us to first try to find our way through a rather problematic document and then to find out that apparently a lot of work was already done at the same time to get a better copy. Then the Chamber was not informed about any intention to apply for protective measures for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Is it true that the revised translation has not yet been filed and up-loaded and is still sent through e-mail?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It has been up-loaded into e-court and sent through e-mail. It has not been filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that it would be better to have it filed, because if there is a translation filed, then I think if there's a new translation, it should be filed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We will do that this afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milas. Please be seated. Mr. Milas, you'll first be examined by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milas.

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: Boris Milas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us what your current occupation is?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: I am an officer with the Croatian Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have 65 ter 1D2699 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, do you recall giving two statements to members of the Defence of Ante Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And looking on your screen, is that your signature on the bottom of the first page?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: Correct, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall being interviewed on three occasions: first, from the 19th to the 23rd of January, 2009; the 3rd through the 6th of February, 2009; and the 19th of May, 2009, by members of the Gotovina Defence?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall signing a statement on the 19th of May, 2009?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review the statement that is on the screen?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Does that statement accurately reflect what you told members of the Gotovina Defence?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: It does reflect accurately what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At the time you gave this statement, did you give it to the best of your knowledge and in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: In accordance with the truth, by all means, and to the best of my knowledge as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I asked you the same questions today in court that you were asked prior to signing the witness statement that's on the screen, would you provide the same answers today in court as you did to the questions that were posed to you during the course of the interview that led to that statement?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: Yes, I would provide the same answers; maybe not word for word, but in essence the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this statement be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1532.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1532 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit 1D2744 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, do you recall meeting with members of the Gotovina Defence on the 20th and 21st of June, 2009?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall signing a statement -- a supplemental statement on the 22nd of June, 2009?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, does this statement reflect, accurately reflect what you told members of the Gotovina Defence on the 20th and 21st of June, 2009?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: It reflects exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At the time you gave this statement, did you give it to the best of your knowledge and in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge and certainly true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I asked you the same questions today in court that you were asked on the 20th and 21st of June, 2009, would you provide the same answers in court today as you did in the statement that's on the screen?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: Yes, I would provide the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 1D2744 be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have an objection to two specific paragraphs of this statement. And may I be permitted to make my submissions? And the witness should not be privy to what I have to say, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's first ask the witness. Mr. Milas, do you speak and/or understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot speak so well to allow me to follow the proceedings without help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it seems that you apparently have a basic knowledge of the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I don't have occasion to speak it very frequently, so I'm not -- I don't have a very large vocabulary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Under those circumstances, since Ms. Mahindaratne would like to raise a matter which should be raised in such a way that the witness would not hear it, which you'll understand, as a lawyer, I have to ask you to leave the courtroom for a while so that we can hear what Ms. Mahindaratne wants to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I object to paragraph 3 of this supplementary statement, particularly the second part of the -- of paragraph 3. There, the witness draws a legal conclusion. He makes an assessment that the number of burnt houses in Sector South was not widespread, and that, I believe, is a matter for the Trial Chamber, apart from which there are different facts -- different figures that have been placed before the Trial Chamber with regard to the number of houses damaged in Sector South. So I believe in that context, paragraph 3 should not be admitted into evidence. My second objection is to paragraph -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we take it step by step. Could we hear from Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Starting with the last argument, Your Honour, that's not an argument at all. She can cross-examine on the number, but that's no reason not to admit something into evidence. If the witness disagrees on the number or whatever Ms. Mahindaratne thinks the true numbers are, she is certainly free to use her time in cross-examination to put it to him, but that's not a bar to admission. Moreover --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, there are two elements in this. Yes, let me first let you finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Moreover, the issue about the legal conclusion, quite frankly, I'm surprised at that comment, because then we will -- Mr. Kehoe and I will go back through every UNMO report, UNCRO report, UNCIVPOL report, witness statement, about widespread and systematic that was put into evidence by the Prosecution. Now, the phrase "widespread and systematic," as the Court is aware, has a certain legal implication to it. This witness said he didn't think it represented a widespread occurrence. Certainly, I think the Prosecution is seeking to eat its cake and have it too, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not spend too much time on it. Ms. Mahindaratne, I think you are, from a legal point of view, from a procedural point of view, you're perfectly right. Nevertheless, we have heard so many witnesses expressing their views, and I'm not telling you what the Chamber is going to do with these views because the Chamber, of course, primarily will focus on facts. Now, what we have here, we have the surface, 6.000 square kilometres. I do not know whether there's any dispute among the parties about that number. You're talking about numbers. We have a surface, and then what you usually have is a population on that surface. And then you have a number of homes on which this population lives, and then you have a number of homes which are burned. And then the next question is: When they were burned, why they were burned? If it was a result of persons setting fire to those homes, who had done this? I mean, it's clear to you that the Chamber would not simply say, Oh, Mr. Milas said it was not like that. Of course, we will analyse carefully. Now, we can do two things: invite Mr. Misetic to see what knowledge this witness has which is at the basis of his conclusion, just as many others, that, I toured the area for three days, or for five days, or, I was only in the eastern part, or, I toured the whole of the area, I saw five villages or 20 villages burnt. Of course, what the Chamber is seeking, and Mr. Misetic is certainly aware of that, is to see that if somebody gives an assessment, which has both a legal connotation and an everyday meaning, whether we are -- have a busy schedule in this courtroom. You could look at it from an administrative point of view, comparing it to other Chambers. You could also say, Well, I find this rather busy, which is an everyday assessment of how you experience that. Now, what would you like us to do, to say, Strike it? And then Mr. Misetic will then surely, I take it, go into the factual basis for such an assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think we're confusing two things here. The witness doesn't say there was no widespread or systematic burning. The issue here is he's the chief of the Crime Prevention Service. A question that certainly could be put to him is, What was your impression, as chief of the service, about the scope of the problem of burning? His response is, It did not seem to me that it was a widespread occurrence. It's his subjective view, and certainly something the Chamber is entitled to hear. He's not stating as a fact that it was or wasn't and that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it will assist or not, and if you say does not lead to the conclusion, of course, that is not establishing that it was not your view --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Ms. Mahindaratne, what are we going to do with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I hear you, Mr. President. I withdraw the objection and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Invite Mr. Misetic to see whether there's any factual basis for his interpretation of what happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That would be up to Mr. Misetic, Mr. President. I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I do intend to put this matter to him, but I do also want to state, Mr. President, that again what I was interested in, with that paragraph, is his explanation of what he saw, and was it a small problem or a big problem. The fact that he uses the word "widespread" I don't think is a legally-binding conclusion on the Chamber in any sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's -- it may be a conclusion to be drawn by the Chamber, but let's -- it seems that Ms. Mahindaratne, being aware of the approach the Chamber will take in respect of this kind of statement, has withdrawn her objection, and you're invited -- well, you don't need even to be encouraged, Mr. Misetic, but you'll pay attention to the factual part of what is underlying this assessment. Second?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in view of the approach the Trial Chamber has indicated as being taken towards this type of statements, I do not wish to object to the other paragraph that I said I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I'd like to know what caused you problems. If you just point at the paragraph, then we might well understand what your problem is, and that Mr. Misetic also knows where he has to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is paragraph 15, again the second part of paragraph 15, where the witness, having stated that he did not have any contact with General Gotovina, either formally or informally, goes on to speculate as to why -- what General Gotovina thought, or what was in his mind, or why he did not act in a certain way. It is mere speculation. That was the only basis I wanted to object to that part of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic is certainly encouraged to verify whether it's speculation or whether there's any basis for the assessments given there. Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. We could invite the witness to return to the courtroom. Since there are no objections against admission of this additional statement anymore, Mr. Registrar, the 2009 statement of Mr. Milas would be number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1533, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, we were able to resolve all outstanding matters. Mr. Misetic will now further examine you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I have explained to the witness the procedure of reading a summary of the evidence. He is aware of it, and with your permission I'd like to read out a summary of the evidence. The booths have been provided with a copy. Witness AG-34, Boris Milas, is an officer in the Croatian Armed Forces. During Operation Storm, he was the head of the Crime Prevention Service of the 72nd Military Police Battalion which operated within the Split Military District. The witness testifies that on the day before Operation Storm began, he participated in a meeting where officials sent from the Military Police Administration in Zagreb were present. During this meeting on the night of 3 August 1995, an order of General Mate Lausic was presented to the witness, which stated that the commanders of the 72nd and 73rd Military Police Battalions were to be subordinated to Major Ivan Juric, who was sent from Zagreb into the field by General Lausic. Furthermore, Captain Ante Glavan, an official from the Crime Investigation Department at the Military Police Administration in Zagreb, was sent from Zagreb by General Lausic, and the witness states that he, the witness, was subordinated to Mr. Glavan, who in turn was subordinated to Major Juric. The witness states that both Major Juric and Mr. Glavan submitted their reports directly to General Lausic and did not report to General Gotovina. The witness states that as the chief of the Crime Prevention Service, he had neither formal nor informal contacts with General Gotovina before or after Operation Storm. The witness testifies that on the 12th of August, 1995, General Lausic's deputy chief, Marijan Biskic, came from Zagreb and met with the members of the 72nd Military Police Battalion. Major Juric reported to Brigadier Biskic that the 72nd Military Police Battalion had completed all scheduled military police tasks during and after Operation Storm, and even more than that. Major Juric stated that members of the 72nd Military Police Battalion needed to be commended for that. During this meeting, Brigadier Biskic issued the tasks that the MPs were to focus on in the coming period of time. The witness testifies that as far as the work segment of the Crime Investigation Military Police is concerned, no approval was required from General Gotovina, nor did General Gotovina have to make a special request in relation to operative and criminal processing. And that concludes the summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, first, if you could explain to the Trial Chamber a little bit about your background. What type of police training did you have before you were appointed the chief of the -- or the head of the Crime Prevention Service?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: Before I joined the 72nd Military Police Battalion, I did not have any experience as a military policeman or as a policeman in a civilian structure, police structure. After I joined the military police, I performed some tasks in an office that was a joint office of the commanders -- the then commander of the 72nd Battalion, who was more involved in writing certain reports and orders. But together with some other officers of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, I also visited some other relocated units of the 72nd Battalion. That is the extent of my police experience and knowledge. Sometime in September 1992, I believe on the 15th of September, 1992, I was appointed the acting head of the Crime Prevention Service of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, and I performed those duties through the end of 1996, when I was reassigned to a -- to another unit of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you have any training in how to conduct investigations, any sort of -- let's say prior to 1995, even after you became the acting chief, did you have any training in terms of how to conduct a criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: I did not undergo any training, nor any on-the-job training in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How about the people that were subordinated to you? Without going into the details of every person, can you give us a general overview about the level of training of the members of the Crime Prevention Service that were beneath you in the chain? What general levels of education and police training did they have?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: There was a total of 12 officers in the Crime Prevention Service when I was appointed to my -- to that post. And of the 12, one was a driver and another one was a woman, an administrative officer. As for the education and training they had undergone, these were people who completed secondary education, and in some cases there were even persons who just underwent crash courses for secondary education. And one of the members, one of the officers, was a lawyer by profession. She had a degree in Law. In other words, they did not have any police education or training, especially not in investigating on-site investigations and crime processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to the Court why the Crime Prevention Service of the 72nd Military Police Battalion did not have -- was not staffed by people with more of an education or training in police matters?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: If you look at the composition of the military police as of its inception in 1992, some -- four and a half thousand to 5.000 staff, 80 per cent of them had a secondary education. To the best of my recollection, only a few of them had some sort of previous police training before joining the police force. Even those who had secondary education, as I said a moment ago, came from different backgrounds. Some of them had completed grammar schools, and others who had completed vocational schools for joiners, carpenters, salespersons, et cetera. At any rate, their education was far from what was compatible with the police duties, in particular those relating to crime investigation. According to the information I have, around 150 staff had an associate degree or university degree education, and I'm referring to the police force in Croatia overall at the time. This was far from sufficient for the duties that had to be taken care of. However, these were men who had left Croatian brigades and joined the police and tried to do their best in discharging their duties. The chief of the Military Police Administration and his assistants intended to develop various levels of education and training over time in order to raise the level of their skills to the satisfactory level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- first, if you could tell us whether you know. Do you know why more people weren't taken from, for example, the civilian police and brought into the military police?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: Well, it was up to someone to take a decision to that effect. The individuals I referred to came to join the military police units voluntarily. It could not be resolved by a commander of a single MP battalion by asking that the Split-Dalmatia Police Administration second ten lawyers or ten economists to join the police force. These were volunteers who -- most of whom had previously been members of the Guards Brigades as of the month of June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, turning your attention to the composition of the Crime Prevention Service of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, and turning your attention to paragraph 1 of your supplemental statement, which is D1533, can you explain to the Court, on the 3rd of August, 1995, how many members of the Crime Prevention Service of the 72nd Military Police Battalion did you have at your disposal for the purpose of conducting criminal investigations?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: According to the establishment of what had by that time been remained [as interpreted] into the Crime Prevention police, there were 62 members who -- or, rather, 65 members were envisaged under the staffing table, but in reality there was 62 of them. Out of these 62, some 10 staff members had administrative jobs, and some 10 of them were forensic officers. I'm referring to all the structural units of the 72nd Battalion; in other words, Zadar, Sibenik, Sinj, and Dubrovnik companies, as well as the Imotski and Metkovic Platoons. Around exactly 42 staff members could be engaged in the conduct of operative criminal investigation which could fall under the jurisdiction of the military courts, and, by the same token, under the jurisdiction of the Military Police Crime Investigation Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, of those 42, can you tell us how many of those 42 could be deployed for use in the areas of what was the former Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: At the time, seven individuals were deployed there, because we had instructions whereby we should set aside a proportional number from the Crime Investigation Service to Knin, since some of the members were assigned to the newly-established Benkovci [phoen] Platoon from the Zadar company. And definitely in the towns of Dubrovnik and Split a certain number of police officers had to be sent to perform military police duties in respect of those men who were then in the area. So the seven individuals were supposed to cover four shifts, and they were assigned to the joint or combined company in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question: Could you have taken all of the men from the Crime Prevention Service that were stationed in Dubrovnik, Split, Imotski and Sinj and moved them into the newly-liberated areas?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: It was not possible to do that because the orders of the Military Police Administration did not specify numbers. But whenever such orders are issued, they refer to a proportionate number. If we have a company numbering 100 men, then roughly 7 members should be assigned who fall under the Crime Section. However, if all the members from Dubrovnik and all those from Split had been assigned to Knin, then there would be nobody left to investigate crimes and disorderly conduct in towns. And, of course, it was a well-known fact that the army was predominantly present in various towns, once they were pulled out from the battle-front. This became evident in the subsequent reports which discussed the perpetration of crimes. My apologies. When we assigned these officers, none of the leadership, meaning the chief of the Military Police Administration or the chief of the Crime Investigation Service, asked that we should assign more officers to the area of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you just tell the Court, very briefly, in August of 1995, after Operation Storm, was there a front-line in the Dubrovnik area, in the southern part of Dalmatia?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: Of course there was. And there existed a danger, as was the case in the Eastern Sector, and that's why the 68th Military Police Battalion was not deployed in the area where Operation Storm was carried out, precisely because of the assessment that there might be combat activities in Dubrovnik area and eastern area in response to the actions launched by the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In addition to HV being in the towns, were HV forces actually deployed in the Dubrovnik area after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, let's turn your attention to the 3rd of August. And you speak of this in your -- both of your statements, but there was a meeting which you reference on the evening of the 3rd of August at which Major Juric and Mr. Glavan were present. Can you please explain to the Court, in your own words, first, where was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: The meeting was held in the forward command post -- relocated command post of the 72nd MP Battalion, in the locality --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... in the late evening hours, Major Juric, Ante Glavan, and Messrs. Maduna and Cicvaric, who were also members of the Military Police Administration came to the meeting, since the commander of the 72nd Battalion asked that a working meeting be held. His assistants were present there, as well as the representative of the administration that I mentioned, and myself. The commander of the 72nd Battalion introduced Major Ivan Juric to everyone, whereupon he presented us with the order by General Lausic of the 2nd of August, 1995, based on which he and the team from the administration were assigned to the 72nd Battalion, because the task given to Major Ivan Juric was that he should be superior to the commander of the 72nd and 73rd MP Battalions, but only for the elements of the forces which participated in the activities involving the 72nd Battalion. If I remember correctly, he was also charged with performing all the military police tasks. And under that same order, he was duty-bound to coordinate with commanders of the Croatian Army in the area of activity, and he was empowered to take all and any measures against commanders if the military police tasks would not be carried out as envisaged under the rules and under the order. In other words, I understood Major Ivan Juric to be the commander of the 72nd Battalion and to also be the commander of those elements of the 73rd Battalion which had at the time been attached to the 72nd. Captain Ante Glavan was the assistant chief of the General Crime Department of the Military Police Administration, and in relation to the Crime Investigation Police of the 72nd Battalion, he was supposed to coordinate all the activities and tasks of the Crime Investigation Military Police and to report to Ivan Juric on all these activities, as well as the representative of the Department of the Criminal Investigation Police, who was at the time Captain --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, first we have to catch two names now. First, would you please repeat the name of the place where this meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: Gornji Rujani. It's the IZM. The order said "Sajkovici," but that's very close by, and it's called Gornji Rujani, and that was the forward command post. That's how I wrote it down. I may have made a mistake, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The second thing we need to clarify is the last part of your answer, which was that Mr. Glavan was supposed to coordinate all the activities and tasks of the Crime Investigation Military Police and to report to Ivan Juric on all these activities, as well as the representative of -- can you repeat the rest of that, including providing us the name?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS
utterances.text: Ante Glavan, to the chief of the Crime Investigation Police of the MP Administration, Spomenko Eljuga, he was the one that Ante Glavan submitted reports to on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I'm looking at the clock. Mr. Milas, we have to adjourn for the day. The courtroom is needed for other cases later today. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. But I'd first like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether the testimony already given today or whether the testimony still to be given tomorrow or perhaps even the day after tomorrow. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may say something before the witness leaves court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The Prosecution wish to hand over some documentation to the witness, simply because it would expedite the examining process tomorrow, particularly cross-examination. We could not hand the documents to the witness. In fact, the initial intimated that he could not communicate with us, but the Witnesses and Victim unit could not trace him yesterday to give the documentation. So with your permission, if the documents could be handed over to the witness. And it's documents that the witness is familiar with and which have been disclosed to the Defence, so it's generally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean disclosed to the Defence in the context of your intended cross-examination or in general terms?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the context of the examination, Mr. President. Let me explain what they are. These are crime registers of the three military police companies, Knin, Zadar and Sibenik, and the corresponding crime reports, as well as three charts which were specifically disclosed to the Defence in the context of the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure -- cross-examination hasn't started of this witness, so I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but this is, of course, a bit of an extraordinary situation, where usually the cross-examining party releases to the party that has called the witness at the time the examination-in-chief has been finished, and of course we have major portions of the evidence of the witness already available as 92 ter statement. So I could imagine that where the Prosecution here is seeking to give documents to the witness, that they had already at an earlier stage than usual already informed the Defence on what material they intended to use during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is not the case, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. In fact, three charts were sent to the Defence last week, with an e-mail saying that those charts would be used in relation to this witness. It was done -- it was a courtesy copy which was sent so the Defence would have ample time to study the charts vis-a-vis the source material. I could perhaps give you the exact date when it was disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I add something here, Your Honour, because we've been concerned, what happened. The materials my learned friend refers to were disclosed on the 29th of May, untranslated registers, under Rules 66 and Rule 68. I was wondering when those materials came into the hands of the Prosecution, because I personally would have liked to have used them in cross-examination of their witnesses, and I've had my own translation team deal with matters for me in respect of them. And now the Prosecution is seeking to put those materials, which were not translated for the Defence, we were not told when they came into their possession, and seeking to put them into the hands of this witness to facilitate their cross-examination. That may be a good thing, but I have been concerned about the practice of disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems, Ms. Mahindaratne, that the issue was far wider, at least that's what I understand from Mr. Kay. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to research right now, the Prosecution is making either 66(B) disclosures or a disclosure that had no reference to any Rule. And I'm reading the e-mail, and it just says: "The attached documents are hereby disclosed to you in relation to Witness Milas."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, that's what I was referring to, and that was a courtesy copy that was sent. It was not a disclosure under Rule 66 nor 68. This was just sent in advance so the Defence would have ample time to study the charts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has this material been disclosed at any earlier stage, not in relation to Mr. Milas?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may explain what these charts are. These are charts produced by the OTP which are just a reproduction of data taken from source material, which are crime registers, which in fact are in evidence, which have been assigned an exhibit number. So Mr. Kay is obviously referring to some other registers and crime reports, most of which are already in evidence. All the Prosecution has done is reproduce data from exhibits onto charts, just the type of charts that Mr. Kay, himself, produced in relation to the organigrams; you know, the structure of the military police. So the charts are in English, and there was no issue about translation. So I think there is a miscommunication. All the Prosecution wished to do was to hand the charts in advance to the Defence so that the Defence would have enough time to study the charts, compare them with the source material, so that we would save court time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let me first say one thing. This is a matter which should not be raised at the time we are supposed to adjourn, Ms. Mahindaratne. This further would be a matter which you should have discussed with the Defence teams to see to what extent you could explain to them what it is, whether there would be any objection against giving it to Mr. Milas. But to start this discussion exactly at 1.45 means that you expose me to heavy criticism from any other Judges. I suggest that you do immediately what I think you would have been supposed to do; that is, to further discuss the matters, because now apparently you are explaining to the Defence what it is, and the Chamber is listening carefully, but it seems to be a wider issue. If the parties cannot agree on whether or not the material could be given to Mr. Milas, the Chamber would like to be informed this afternoon, because it doesn't make much sense to wait until tomorrow, because it would miss your point if the matter were to be decided only later today. And if need be, the Chamber, or I, as Presiding Judge, would be willing to meet with the parties. That would not be a formal part of the trial, but just a meeting to see whether I can assist the parties in resolving the matter, and giving them some guidance. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- acceptable to everyone? I'm also looking at the accused, because usually the Chamber does not meet with the parties outside court, but I have difficulties to imagine that you would oppose against such a meeting, if need be. We adjourn for the day. I've given you my instructions, Mr. Milas. We'll resume tomorrow, 9.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of June, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.55 p.m.,
